title: Notes of Ministry - 74 - January 1979

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 74 - January 19 (2043)/Notes of Ministry - 74 - Januar - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire, beloved brethren, to say a word tonight about spiritual prosperity. There is such a thing as material prosperity, and we recognise the principle of stewardship in regard to material prosperity, manifesting itself in hospitality and the support of the Lord’s interests.

But I wanted to speak tonight of what is greater, and that is spiritual prosperity. There are none of us I am sure but what would desire to prosper spiritually. It is a certain desire that is brought out by the Holy Spirit—the desire to prosper spiritually, and I thought that these scriptures might be a help to all of us in the fulfilment of that desire.

It has always been a matter of interest to me that the books of Psalms, so rich in experience and so rich in spiritual substance, should begin as they do. You look at the verse, “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the wicked, and standeth not in the way of sinners, and sitteth not in the seat of scorners”, and you may wonder why the books of Psalms, so rich in types of the Lord Jesus Christ, so wonderful in the experiences that they give, should begin with that verse. What it brings out, beloved brethren, is a great principle, and that is that experience spiritually is only profitable to persons who have some exercise as to a sanctified walk. I lay that before the brethren as a first principle in regard to spiritual prosperity, the need for a sanctified walk. Of course we are all thankful for divine grace that has ensured to us, even in these days of brokenness, spiritual companionship. We are thankful for that. But the Spirit of God would give us at the beginning of the books of Psalms all these negative thoughts in regard to a person who does not walk in a certain way, and I would leave that with all the brethren, particularly the younger brethren, as to the need for a sanctified walk, in relation to companionships, in relation to friendships, in relation to social links, if there is to be spiritual prosperity.

Then it says, “But his delight is in Jehovah’s law, and in his law doth he meditate day and night”. The law here, in our time, would undoubtedly refer to the Holy Scriptures. It would involve in our time both the Old and New Testaments. Another great principle in soul prosperity is the valuing of the Holy Scriptures. “His delight is in Jehovah’s law”; that is confirmatory of a thought that came before us yesterday, that a person’s heart be engaged.

Beloved, when you read the Holy Scriptures is your heart engaged, are your affections engaged? I have often been affected in reading Mr. Darby’s ‘Synopsis’ how often he breaks out in holy feelings, as if his heart is engaged. The psalmist delights in Jehovah’s law.

Beloved brethren, as you read the gospels of Luke and John, as you meditate on Jehovah’s law, do you delight in it? Is there something surging up in your soul in the way of spiritual feeling and appreciation of the glory of that blessed Man who is delineated in the pages of Scripture? What a touch of spiritual prosperity it is when you delight, when your affections are engaged with the living character of the Holy Scriptures.

Then he says, “In his law doth he meditate day and night”, and that brings out the mind, brings out the faculty of thinking. Think of the wonders of Scripture, the wonders of what is unfolded in the ways of God, the purposes of God, what concerns Israel, what concerns the assembly, what concerns the world to come and concerns eternity, and you meditate on these things. It all adds up to soul prosperity. So that you delight in Jehovah’s law, in that your affections are drawn out; it is not as you would read a text book, or a manual of instruction from the college, your delight is in Jehovah’s law. I have been very exercised for myself (I hope the brethren will forgive me for referring to what I have been exercised in) that I should not use the Holy Scriptures just as a text book for preaching or ministry, but should use the Holy Scriptures to feed my soul.

Then it says, “He is as a tree planted by brooks of water”—an evident allusion to the Holy Spirit. It does not say ‘by a river’; it says “by brooks of water”. Scripture never makes a distinction without a difference. The thought of a river refers to the Holy Spirit in a broad, general sense, but the brook—and this is where the current, practical side comes to us—refers to the present, living flow of the Holy Spirit as it reaches me. Are we like trees drawing our sustenance continually from the blessed Spirit? It brings up the whole question as to how near we are to the blessed source of refreshment currently in the blessed Spirit, bearing upon us, not dispensationally exactly, but in our daily lives and experience. Then, “Which giveth its fruit in its season”—very fine that! You think of the Lord Jesus as a Boy in the temple at Jerusalem; how delightful was the fruit in its season! How beautiful the fruit in its season also in older brethren who have mellowness of spirit, the choice result of experience with God. What an asset older brethren are in a company, marked by “fruit in its season”.

Then it says “whose leaf fadeth not”. Elder brethren in a locality should be concerned, in a shepherdly spirit, to discern when the leaf is fading. A leaf fades because something has come in to rob it of its freshness and to detach it from the living spring of things. The evidence of the leaf fading may manifest itself in less of a desire for the Holy Scriptures. The shepherds in a locality (Paul exhorts them in Acts 20) exercise vigilance to see that the leaf does not fade. Finally it says, “and all that he doeth prospereth”—spiritual prosperity. What a blessed thing!

It is just like Joseph—he added a touch of prosperity to every circumstance. You go to visit an old sister; you give a touch of prosperity. You come to the service of God—a touch of prosperity. You come to the care meeting; you give a touch of prosperity. “All that he doeth prospereth”. Why? Because the soul is prospering, meditates in the law of Jehovah, and is planted by the brooks of water. Let us cultivate this matter of our personal links with Christ and with the Holy Spirit, with a constant desire for the living word of God that will manifest itself in the leaf never fading, but being in constant greenness and freshness amongst us.

So in John’s gospel the Lord said, “If ye abide in me”. Do you know what it is to abide in Christ? Much has been said about this passage, but what does it mean to abide in Christ? I will put it simply. A person who abides in Christ relates everything to Christ. That is the principle of abiding in Christ. There is not a matter that comes up but you relate it to Christ.

Selfishness takes many forms, and there is no greater obstacle to soul prosperity. One form is relating matters to yourself. How does this affect me? How does it affect my interests? How does it affect my sphere of things? “Ye abide in me” means that you relate every matter to Christ.

Then the Lord says, “and my words abide in you”. Well, “my words” is a different thought from the Scriptures. “Jehovah’s law” and ‘my words” are not the same thing. “My words” means that you are diligent, and you are listening to what the Lord is currently saying amongst His people. “My words abide in you”—there is what you get yourself from the Scriptures, what you get for your own soul’s prosperity, but “my words abide in you” is a reference to His present, living voice, but of course still from the Scripture. It is a good thing, beloved brethren, before you come to a meeting for ministry, or any meeting of that character, to get down before the Lord and ask Him to give you grace to perceive the word that is for you. How good to get on your knees before the meeting and say, ‘Lord help me to discern the word that is for me’. It may be a word bearing on the saints collectively. It abides in you and adds to your prosperity, and it will give you an understanding of the Lord’s interest in the assembly. So you can pray, as it says, “Ye shall ask what ye will and it shall come to pass to you. In this is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit, and ye shall become disciples of mine” (John 15: 7, 8).

What is the fruitfulness that John speaks of here, that God is glorified? Fruit in John’s gospel, in which God is glorified, is “love amongst yourselves”. And one great evidence of soul prosperity is, that we seek, as abiding in Christ, and His word abiding in us, to love the brethren. There is need currently amongst us for an increase in love. The current voice of the Spirit is love, love amongst the brethren. Thereby God is glorified, if there is love amongst the brethren, and it will only come about as we are spiritually prospered by abiding in Christ, His word abiding in us and finding a resting place as we accept it.

This is a very interesting scripture in Colossians 1: 7. I suggest to the brethren that there is some correspondence between Epaphras and Elisha. I do not think there is anything recorded in the scriptures as to what Elisha ministered. The prophetic ministry of Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and many of the minor prophets is recorded, but there is no record in Scripture as to what Elisha ministered and there is no record in Scripture as to what Epaphras said. There are details in Scripture as to what he did, so in that way he represents, in a certain sense, features of Elisha. Elisha’s service was almost entirely conducted in proximity to the Jordan, and power amongst the brethren on the part of any person is in the measure in which they keep near to the Jordan. Jordan is a source of power for a servant. The truth of the death of Christ is a source of power for a servant. Death is the resolving of every issue in a locality, or generally, or in an individual. Death is the solution of every matter. I do not know, beloved brethren, if we fully appreciate the significance of that. Elisha derived his power in relation to the Jordan (2 Kings 2: 13, 14).

“Epaphras … who is a faithful minister of Christ for you, who has also manifested to us your love in the Spirit”. This links with John’s gospel, “your love in the Spirit”. Why did Paul say this? I will tell you why he said it, beloved brethren. This has often been spoken of as a ‘danger epistle’ or an epistle of crisis. They were going on to God’s full thoughts, and the enemy was endeavouring to divert them because they were prosperous (Colossians 1: 6).

Beloved brethren, when the Lord is prospering you locally, that is the time to watch. Epaphras knew that things were prospering in Colosse. They were set for the full thing, so he combated earnestly in prayer (Colossians 4: 12). As we are prospered, beloved brethren, let us be more dependent than ever. If you are prospered individually, be more dependent on God than ever you have been. If you are prospered in your locality, and I can see the evidence of prosperity, beloved brethren, watch. Watch as you have never watched before and be dependent. Epaphras, Paul says, “has also manifested to us your love in the Spirit”. The essential characteristic of love in the Spirit is purity. In localities there are always dangers of partisanship, dangers of diverse feelings, so let there be a demonstration of “love in the Spirit”, in its purity, its unfeigned character, and its unprejudiced character. Thus there will be fruitfulness continuing amongst God’s people.

So Paul prayed: “For this reason we also … do not cease praying and asking for you, to the end that ye may be filled with the full knowledge of his will, in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so as to walk worthily of the Lord unto all well-pleasing, bearing fruit in every good work, and growing by the true knowledge of God”; and Epaphras was in full support. Well, the Lord wants us to prosper individually; He wants us to prosper in our localities, and there are great resources available to us by which that can be achieved, but they are hidden resources, they are the resources that lie in the Spirit. The great feature in Colossians is what is hid, “your life is hid with the Christ in God” (Colossians 3: 3). The Lord would direct us to these hidden things by which we can be maintained in spiritual prosperity.
Again I say brethren, in all affection, Watch, and ensure that “love in the Spirit” is what can be said to mark you, as I would seek that it might be said of where I come from, for His name’s sake.

Luke 8: 15; 11: 34–36; 24: 45–I thought we might profitably continue the subject of trustworthiness and how, from another standpoint, we might see the kind of persons the Lord can trust. There is a sense in which the Lord leaves things to us even if we are not trustworthy. The fact of the matter is that things get into our hands in any case. The Lord speaks about the faithful steward (Luke 12: 42), but there were also those who were unfaithful in that chapter. They were left with his interests, his matters; they took on responsibility for them. Some were unfaithful, but some were faithful. So we would desire to be faithful stewards, that is, worthy of the Lord’s trust.

In this parable of the sower there were four different kinds of ground. It brings in the side of our responsibility. We were looking at John’s gospel and the side of sovereignty, God’s sovereign operations in new birth. There would be no one worthy of trust without God’s sovereign operations—that is one side of the matter. But here it is a matter of the ground, the soil, and that would bring in responsibility. We are responsible to provide certain soil for the seed. The seed is the word of God, and God is active in His word. It is a question of having ears to hear, of providing soil that the word may fall into and produce fruit. Only one of these four kinds of soil brings forth fruit to perfection. There is the wayside, which is hardened soil, where the seed is unable to sink in or to penetrate. It suggests a crust of casualness and carelessness, with no crevice for the seed to get in. Then there is the rocky ground. As it says in another version, there is no depth of earth, there is merely superficiality. There seems to be joy but in time of trial persons fall away. Tests will come as to whether the word of God has taken root or has not. This would apply to receiving the word initially, but it would also apply to believers, because God would give us His word continually. Not only do we provide soil at the beginning of our soul history, but we are meant to provide suitable soil all through our lives as the word of God comes to us continually. The Lord speaks in chapter 4 about man living by every word of God (Luke 4: 4). Therefore the believer is to hear the word of God not only initially but continually.

The great test is the kind of soil. There is that which falls where the thorns are. We know what cares and riches and pleasures are. These choke the word so that it is unproductive. This would also apply to believers as to whether the word is effective when it comes to us. But then this fourth kind of soil is “an honest and good heart”. It is a matter of being frank and honest, not pretending anything, not being superficial, but being genuine and exercised. The good ground does not come automatically; it does not come without exercise, and honestly facing what the word conveys. The absence of pretension, the honest and good heart, is what is needed, keeping the word. The Lord says in John 14 “He that has my commandments and keeps them …” (John 14: 21). We are to keep His commandments, value them, treasure them, and be exercised to answer to them. This is the honest and good heart, which would provide an answer to the word of God when it comes to us. “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Luke 4: 4); the believer is meant to live by God’s word. His word, the logos, is what the expression of His mind is.

We would never know the mind of God apart from His word. The Lord Jesus Himself is the Word. He is the full expression of what is in the mind of God. Men would never know what is in God’s mind apart from the Logos, and God is constantly expressing what is in His mind.

The great need is for ears to hear what He is saying—good ground will “bring forth fruit with patience”. It involves exercise and endurance, and overcoming difficulties; not being turned aside or deflected, but bringing forth fruit with patience. It is meant to be a continual exercise with us that we should provide this good ground, so there would not only be satisfaction for believers, but fruit for God, an answer to what He may express as to His mind at any time.

We often speak as if it were difficult to get God’s mind. In one sense it is, but that is because of difficulties with us. There is no difficulty on God’s side. God would not deprive us of His mind; He would not from His side make it difficult. If anyone of us would with an honest and good heart desire to have God’s mind about any matter, especially as to His interests, He would tell us what His mind is. The difficulty is on our side. We may be governed by preference or prejudice, whereas the honest and good heart has no ulterior motive, no other object, but is genuine and real; the word is received and kept, and it brings forth fruit with patience. We are all responsible as believers to provide this good ground in our own links with the Father, with the Lord Jesus, and with the Holy Spirit. The good ground is what we are meant to provide, that the word is received, and there is an answer to it for God’s pleasure.

In chapter 11 of this gospel we have the idea of the eye being simple. The eye being simple is very much like the honest and good heart. “The lamp of the body is thine eye—when thine eye is simple, thy whole body also is light; but when it is wicked, thy body also is dark”. It is how the light is received. The inlet for the light is the eye, and it is needful that the eye be simple; not complicated, not occupied with other things, but simple in the sense of being single as to object; not having many objects, but having one object. The Lord Jesus is to be the believer’s object. The eye is to be on Him, and on light from Him. “Thy whole body … is light” is what every one of us would desire to have, “not having any part dark”; not any obscure part somewhere, which will be so if the eye is not simple. It would involve the exposure of ourselves, the judging of ourselves. The light would do that so that there is no part dark. It is a very interesting possibility for every one of us. Just as the good ground is individual, this also is a matter of our own soul’s relations with God.

Joseph in the beginning of Matthew’s gospel was uncertain. He was not sure what to do regarding Mary. He was unwilling to expose her publicly, and purposed to put her away secretly. It says in verse 20 of Matthew 1—“while he pondered on these things”. We tend to consult with another. This was a real difficulty, a real problem in Joseph’s life, but he did not consult with anyone else. He pondered. He did not do anything immediately; he would be praying about it, have his own soul’s relations with God about it; he pondered. It illustrates the honest and good heart, and the simple eye; and while he pondered the angel of God appeared to him. There is an answer while he pondered. We might get on the telephone with somebody else, or write to somebody else—he pondered on these things. This needs to be developed as a habit with us that when things confront us we know how to ponder. Nehemiah, in a certain difficulty, consulted with himself (Nehemiah 5: 7). He would be before God individually first; and then he remonstrated with others afterwards. The danger is to consult with others and be diverted or deflected, to follow somebody else’s idea, whereas the great need is honesty in our own relations with God. If a person honestly and with a simple eye gets before God, God will not withhold His mind regarding any particular matter. I am sure this is an important guide. Of course we have all failed; we all know what it is to consult others and get ourselves involved. We accepted things we should not have accepted. We should have learned these lessons in the past, and learn to be individually before God and derive His mind from Him. He will not withhold His mind from any one who is honest and simple as to his objective. Now such persons become trustworthy because they have their own link with God, and God can trust them, and they are worthy of His trust because they are persons to whom He can disclose His mind.

In Luke 24 there is the great matter of understanding; “Then he opened their understanding to understand”. This is greatly needed in our day. The Lord was about to leave the disciples and they were to remain in the city. This was a current matter existing at that time; and He opened their understanding to understand. In the day in which we are there are sometimes difficulties.

The disciples thought things were difficult here. The word perplexity comes in in verse 4. We all know what it is to be in perplexity, but how good to have our understanding opened to understand. We need to understand God’s mind for us at the present juncture in the testimony. There is a certain setting in which we are, and it is important to understand it. It says here “He opened their understanding to understand the scriptures”. The Lord opened their understanding. It is what He does, and it is not only individual, it is collective too in a sense, to understand the position in which they were at the moment. The Spirit had not yet come; the Lord was about to leave them, and the promise of the Father was about to come upon them, but they were to remain in the city. They did that intelligently; they knew exactly where they were at that particular juncture. And it is good for us to know where we are. They did not arrive at this by their own efforts or by their own study. They had failed; they had disbelieved and were in perplexity, but the Lord so acts in his gathering. His shepherding care, that they were found together, and the Lord leaves them as a company who are committed to Him intelligently. We need to wait on the Lord that He will open our understanding as to the situation in which we are at this moment.

There is no doubt at all that the disciples loved the Lord. Even when they failed—even when Peter failed—they still had intense love for Christ. But while we are to have love for the Lord Jesus and be maintained in that, we need also intelligence. The Lord would have us not only affectionate but intelligent. We would give hundreds of thousands of believers on this earth credit for loving the Lord, but I wonder how many of us are really intelligent as the Lord would have us be. May the Lord help us all to understand, to be concerned to provide this good ground, this honest and good heart. May we be maintained with this simple eye, and may we have our understanding opened.

It is to interested persons that the Lord would grant the opening of their understanding. If we are not really interested, we will not get our understandings opened, but if we are really set and interested in this direction the Lord will be pleased to open our understanding so that we understand, and are believers here who are marked by genuine affection for Christ and who also have understanding.

articles.title: “I WILL POUR MY SPIRIT UPON THY SEED”
articles.author: N. T. Meek
articles.meeting: Substance of word in meeting for ministry

paragraphs.text: This scripture refers to God’s dealings with the remnant of Israel in a future day, and they are presented from God’s side. I would like, however, to apply it to our own day as suggesting God’s acting in relation to the children and young people among us—“thy seed” and “thine offspring”.

It is of all moment that young believers should have the gain of the Spirit’s presence and I have wondered whether we who are older, and parents particularly, may tend to overlook this important matter. We are rightly concerned that the children should know the forgiveness of sins and be sheltered by the precious blood of Jesus, and many are the prayers that go up in this relation. But perhaps we are not so urgent as to their receiving the Holy Spirit. A young believer may show but little taste for the Scriptures. It may be difficult with some to sustain a conversation as to the Lord Jesus. Interest in the meetings and in the ministry may be spasmodic and the outlook may trend toward the world. It is a question whether such have got the gain of the Spirit’s presence.

We may urge the young to ask for the Spirit for themselves. They have their own responsibility to do so. But perhaps, along with this, parents, and all of us, should be more diligent to invoke God’s promise here, “I will pour my Spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thy offspring”. Personally, one feels one has been concerned almost exclusively as to their eternal salvation, but in truth their reception of, and their getting the gain of, the Spirit is essential if they are to develop in a normal way. We who are older are not without responsibility for them; they are regarded as thy seed, thine offspring.

We should look for evidences of the Spirit’s presence and working. An inclination to be in the company of the Lord’s people, a question as to the meaning of a scripture, some personal reading of the precious ministry, are all encouraging signs that the Spirit is gaining a place in a young believer’s life. May we water these evidences, perhaps small in their beginnings, with earnest prayer.

I am sure that some young ones stand in very real need of the personal gain of the Spirit’s presence. We should not fail to urge them to ask for this great gift. From our side we may have prayed long for their conversion, and in due time this may have come about. May we be prepared to travail again that the joy, outlook, and spiritual tastes which flow from the Spirit’s presence may also be their portion.

Exodus 25: 2, 8, 9; 35: 29; 34: 1, 2 (to “for the morning”), 4, 10–12 (to “come”); 40: 34–What is in mind is to speak about the sanctuary—a heave-offering and the sanctuary. The heave-offering involves our affections. God has in mind in this chapter that He might have dwelling conditions among His people, a dwelling-place, and the appeal is to our affections.

The proposal is that the saints in their affections will provide dwelling conditions for God. So the word is, “Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring me a heave-offering: of every one whose heart prompteth him, ye shall take my heave-offering”. What develops in the book affords an outlet for our affections, regulated affections; affections moving rightly is what one has in mind, as we find in the rest of this book. It was said in the reading that there may be profession of love for Christ, but associated with evil; but what this section brings out is God’s appeal to our affections and the importance of our affections being regulated. God having in mind that the affections of His saints would rise to the opportunity, that they would make Him a sanctuary.

There are two words used—the footnote to the word “sanctuary” (Exodus 25: 8) says, ‘holy as to place’, then the word “tabernacle” (Exodus 25: 9) means ‘habitation’, God having in mind to be amongst His people, securing dwelling conditions amongst His saints. Solomon said, “But will God indeed dwell on the earth?”, 1 Kings 8: 27. The question is raised as if it were incredible that God should dwell with men. Well, what is the answer? Revelation 21 is the answer; He will dwell eternally with men by means of the tabernacle, the assembly, “the tabernacle of God is with men, and he shall tabernacle with them” (Revelation 21: 3)—that is the answer to Solomon’s question. There is no incredibility—this book shows just the very opposite. It is a prime thing in the heart and mind of God that there should be conditions secured amongst the saints that will provide Him with a dwelling place.

So the heave-offering is described. It springs from the affections, but it is not anything—no, it is all prescribed, the materials necessary for the composition, the construction of a dwelling place for God. He says, “And they shall make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them”.

Think of God’s desire! What was said then will be secured eternally—by means of the assembly God will be near to men. But then in Ephesians 2, as to Ephesus, Paul is saying, “in whom”—that is, in Christ, in the Lord—“ye also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2: 22). God is here in the Spirit at the moment. You would think that Exodus 25 was the first reference to it, but if we go back to Exodus 15 we find that Moses and the children of Israel speak about the thing as an accomplished fact. There was nothing built and as yet no suggestion from God, but the saints in their song speak about the sanctuary, the place that His hands had prepared. Well, that would be light, I suppose. The saints seemed to apprehend what God had in mind and spoke of it as if it were accomplished.
I suppose they were looking right on, you might say, to Solomon’s day—the saints in the land, the house built, and the glory in residence.

Now, dear brethren, I believe that though that was light, there was something that corresponded in the saints. We read in Psalm 114 that when Israel went out of Egypt “Judah was his sanctuary, Israel his dominion”. How do we explain it? There was something in the saints that corresponded with the light of God’s thoughts. Possibly that was related to the cloud, because we get the cloud in chapter 14 before there was the tabernacle—a protective element. So in the book of Exodus we get the tabernacle, we get the pattern, but as yet nothing made. Then we get the breakdown; then we get recovery; then we get the pattern over again, and then the thing brought to pass—that is the book of Exodus. So, “they shall make me a sanctuary”. God had in mind that there would be conditions amongst the saints that would be suitable to His presence “that I may dwell among them”. And all was to be “according to … the pattern”.

In Exodus 34 we read about the two tables. What I had in mind as to that scripture is simply this, that it indicates that God is going on with His thoughts. The breakdown has just come in, nevertheless God is going on with His thoughts. They are unchanged, they are unaffected by the ruin. His thoughts, His mind, are the same. So the two tables are made, like the first. Then in Exodus 35 there is a fresh appeal for the heave-offering, a fresh appeal to the affections of the saints. What that chapter brings out is the full answer in the saints, God’s willing people, the wise-hearted and the willing-hearted, their affections rising to the divine mind, answering to God’s desire, and providing more than enough, so that in chapter 36 they had to be restrained.

I refer to these scriptures as indicating just what God is after in the way of willingness, and wisdom too. Both these elements are in chapter 35. So it says, “This is the word which Jehovah has commanded, saying, Take from among you a heave-offering to Jehovah—every one whose heart is willing, let him bring it, Jehovah’s heave-offering” (Exodus 36: 4, 5). Then it says, “The children of Israel brought, a voluntary offering to Jehovah, every man and woman whose heart prompted them to bring for all manner of work, which Jehovah, by the hand of Moses, had commanded to be done”. There it is, the answer in the saints. All the material necessary is at hand; nothing is yet built, but all the material is available. What stimulation is in that for you and me; God is going on with His thoughts despite the breakdown, cherishing His own thought that He would have dwelling conditions amongst His people. Then we get four chapters, 36 to 39, of labour, of work, and everything is made, and everything conforms to the pattern.

We read the word in chapter 34, “Behold, I make a covenant—before all thy people I will do marvels that have not been done in all the earth, nor in any nation; and all the people in the midst of which thou art shall see the work of Jehovah”, and then, “Take heed to thyself, that thou make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land”. I am impressed by these two references—first, God committing Himself to deal with their enemies, committing Himself to it on the basis of a covenant—that is our God. That is 1 Corinthians 1: 9, “God is faithful”.

No matter what has come in, “God is faithful”. That is His side of the covenant. But then there is our side, “make no covenant …”. The covenant is the bond between God and His people and admits of no other covenant. I say this, dear brethren, in relation to what is in mind; it is all on the way to dwelling conditions for God. “Make no covenant”—trade unions, professional associations—no other covenant is admitted in the light of the bond between God and His people. I just refer to it because it is on the way to what is to be secured for God Himself.

Then, as I said, you get these four chapters of work, everything done, everything made, but not yet put together. You get the sanctuary first of all—the curtains and the boards, in that order. If you or I were building a house we would start on the foundations, build the walls, and put the roof on, would we not? But the order that is given is the curtains and then the boards and then the bases. Why is that, dear brethren? We have been taught that the curtains are the principles; the boards are the persons; the curtains take precedence. Is that not what we were speaking about earlier in 2 Timothy—the principles? There are four of them in 2 Timothy 2: 22—“righteousness, faith, love, peace”—the principles; then the persons, “those that call upon the Lord out of a pure heart”. What is in one’s mind is that these things are all on the way to dwelling conditions for God being realised among the saints.

In Exodus 37 we get the ark, the table, the candlestick, the furnishings internally; it is all on the way to what we have in mind—the sanctuary, a habitation for God. Nothing is put together so far; it is instruction for us as to what is involved in this matter of there being a sanctuary, a habitation for our God. Then we get the court in chapter 38, and then in chapter 39 we have the garments of Aaron and his sons—how much could be said about them. These are four chapters of labour; as I said, things not yet put together, but all there, conforming fully to the pattern. How important that our affections should be set in this direction, regulated in this way, and how important that there should be wisdom so that our affections are in right channels, all on the way to a habitation for God.

In chapter 40 Moses is told to put the whole tabernacle together, to set it up—and then we are told that he did set it up, all according to commandment. There are eight references in chapter 40 to “as Jehovah had commanded”. All is set up, conforming fully to the divine thoughts. It was said in the reading that the work of God by the Spirit conforms perfectly to God’s designs in love, His purpose. How wonderful! Well, the point is this—is that our standard? Is the pattern the thing that regulates us? Is this what we have before us? God has His own objective in His purpose and in His ways, but He realises His purpose by means of His ways in His operations by the Spirit in your heart and in mine. That is how the thing will come about, by His subjective operations by the Spirit. But then, on the other hand, we need to recognise that God has a standard. He is not content with anything—He has His pattern and the obligation is upon us to go by the pattern.

So we find that the tabernacle is set up, and then the glory fills it. There was the pattern, then the breakdown, then recovery. That is what we had in London—things reached on the basis of recovery, recovered persons, and God securing an answer in them, an answer to His original thought that He should have dwelling conditions among His saints. So there it is, the thing set up, and it says, “the glory of Jehovah filled the tabernacle”. I think the glory in that sense is the indication of divine approval. Well, how we would covet to have a sense of that, individually and collectively, a sense of divine approval. We will have it in the measure in which our affections are right, undivided, and pure, on the one hand, and on the other hand regulated so that things conform fully to the divine pattern.

So it says, “The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of Jehovah filled the tabernacle. And Moses could not enter into the tent of meeting, for the cloud abode on it, and the glory of Jehovah filled the tabernacle”. There is a certain finality about that. In Hebrews 8: 2 we read about “the true tabernacle, which the Lord has pitched”. I think this would be the foreshadowing of it. Moses, could we say, typical of Christ in this chapter as the One who pitched the true tabernacle. I judge that is the testimonial position at the present time. I judge that the pitching took place in Acts 2; the thing was pitched there. I think there is the foreshadowing of that in this chapter in which God signified His approval of what had come about in the affections and in the labours of His people.

Labour is a Corinthian word. “Your toil”, Paul says—local toil. He says, “Your toil is not in vain in the Lord”, 1 Corinthians 15: 58. What does that mean? “In the Lord” refers to His dominical name, which bears upon our position down here. There is a sphere here where that authority, that dominical name, operates. Is it operating in my heart? That is what it means.

Paul says, “So then, my beloved brethren, be firm, immovable, abounding always in the work of the Lord”—that is Exodus 36 to 39—“knowing that your toil is not in vain in the Lord”. It is God’s willing people, God’s wise-hearted people, answering fully to His thoughts in relation to His being amongst them in conditions suited to Himself. So, as I said, the thing is there, put up, a foreshadowing of “the true tabernacle, which the Lord has pitched, and not man”. There it is, filled with the glory—God signifying His approval of what had come about responsively, and all stemming from the affections of the saints rising to the occasion and answering God’s appeal to them. May the Lord bless the word.

HEAVEN’S VIEW OF THE WORK In Nehemiah 3 we have the divine record of those who worked in the repair of the ruined wall and gates of Jerusalem. So today heaven takes note of each one who is working to maintain the truth and to hold to divine principles. The record in Nehemiah tells us who worked, where they worked, what they did, and in some cases how they did it—one man is said to have “earnestly repaired” not only one piece, but a second piece of the wall. Wherever the Lord has set you—perhaps in a very isolated position—His eye is upon you approvingly as He sees you committed to this labour. He knows every detail of the circumstances and the tests, maybe the opposition, which you face, and would strengthen you to work on, “knowing that your toil is not in vain in the Lord”, 1 Corinthians 15: 58.

It is all well, all that befalls us under the good hand of the Lord Jesus Christ. I make no exceptions of any kind for myself, or for those I love in Him. Surely some ray from His eye gilds every passing sorrow, every trial, thorn, sharp flint, every anguish of mind or body.
Nothing reaches us save as having passed through the jealous flame of His love, and that makes all shine to us that believe.
‘Ministry of G. V. Wigram’ Vol. 3, p.23
